text: School success and difficulty are becoming more personally meaningful.
Success and failure can begin to feel like information about who they are, not only what happened.
They are increasingly aware that classmates have different strengths.
They may compare their speed, skill, knowledge, or popularity with peers.
Friendships are becoming more stable and can carry stronger emotional weight.
They are learning that rules can have reasons, not only consequences.
They can sustain attention on a chosen task longer than younger children, especially when interested.
They increasingly notice whether practice changes their performance.
They are beginning to distinguish between being unable to do something yet and being unable to do it at all.
They may care strongly about fairness, especially when rules seem inconsistent.
They are becoming more capable of explaining what they think happened in a disagreement.
They are developing preferences for subjects, games, hobbies, and ways of learning.
They may seek recognition from teachers, coaches, parents, or other respected adults.
They can become more self-critical when a skill matters to them.
They increasingly understand that other people can have different knowledge or perspectives.
They are learning how groups establish roles, rules, and belonging.
They can take pride in contributing to household or group responsibilities.
They are beginning to understand that effort and strategy can change outcomes.
They may become frustrated when a desired skill develops more slowly than expected.
They are increasingly able to plan a simple sequence toward a goal.
They can use feedback more effectively when it is specific and actionable.
They are learning to recover socially after ordinary disagreements.
They are developing stronger preferences about privacy, possessions, and personal space.
They may enjoy collecting facts or becoming unusually knowledgeable about a favorite subject.
They are increasingly able to notice patterns in their own successes and difficulties.
